newsitem.title: TURKEY: JCR Turkey downgrade will not hit funding - minister.
newsitem.headline: JCR Turkey downgrade will not hit funding - minister.

text.p: The downgrade of Turkey's yen debt by Japan Credit Rating Agency (JCR) should not cause the country difficulties with its future borrowing, State Minister Ufuk Soylemez, said.

"The downgrading was not a surprise. JCR had put Turkey on credit monitor in May and the downgrading had been expected for a while," Soylemez, in charge of the Treasury and privatisation, told Reuters.
JCR Announced Tuesday a downgradeof yen and euroyen bonds issued by Turkey to BB from BB+ and removed the country from credit monitor.

JCR said Turkey's overall macroeconomic situation, buffeted by inflation, external debt servicing obligations, and budget and current account deficits, had been deteriorating despite strong government efforts.
A government official said "The JCR downgrading would not close the way for Turkey to borrow in Japanese markets. Maybe our borrowing costs might rise".
News of the downgrade came the same day as Turkey announced a 750 million mark five year eurobond with a 7.625 coupon.
Turkey has also set a five-year Samurai bond issue worth 75 billion yen and two Euroyen issue of 40 billion yen this year.

Despite the bearish sentiment sparked by the JCR move on the Istanbul Stock Exchange (ISE) where shares fell nearly three percent this morning, Soylemez believes the latest five-year bond issue reflects the confidence of international markets in the Turkish economy.

Soylemez said Turkey's foreign borrowing in international capital markets -- $2.8 billion so far this year -- might rise to $3 billion by the end of 1996 if Turkey finalises negotiations for several deals for smaller amounts.
Turkey has also raised $2 billion this year by selling foreign currency denominated bonds to domestic banks.
"Turkey has secured enough to meet its foreign debt servicing through to the end of January," he said.
Soylemez did not clarify ongoing foreign borrowing deals, but government officials say the Treasury has received some offers for new deals in yen, mark and dollar.
Earlier this year, Turkey had set three Euromark issues totalling 1.1 billion marks -- two of them with a maturity of four years and one with a five-year maturity.

Its previous issue in September carried a coupon of eight percent and a spread of 304 basis points with a maturity of four years. The coupon rate was set at 7.625 percent and spread at 280 basis points at Tuesday's five-year deal.
Turkish banks, on the other hand, have raised some $1.9 billion mainly through syndicated loan deals this year.
"We don't have any bottleneck in foreign and domestic borrowing. The effect of high foreign borrowing will be seen on domestic borrowing interest rates," Soylemez said.
Treasury officials say Turkey is now seeking to extend the average maturity of its domestic debt stock -- 306 days presently.
Turkey has prsently a Ba3 rating from Moody's and B+ from Standard & Poor's (S&P). Both agencies had warned Turkey in July against the deterioration in the fiscal balance.
S&P had also put Turkey under CreditWatch.
Turkish bankers say Moody's and S&P might wait for the result of Turkey's talks with the International Monetary Fund before revising the country's debt rating.
After a two-week assessment visit in October, an IMF team said talks with Turkey would resume in early 1997.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's government unveiled ambitious economic targets under a zero-deficit 1997 budget draft, based on hopes of high privatisation revenues. Economists say the targets are unrealistic.
Turkey is planing to speed up its stagnant privatisation programme which has raised $3.1 billion since it was launched in 1986. The government put three state banks on sale on Monday.
Erbakan is expected to unveil its third revenue-raising package this week. The package will probably include privatisation of power plants.
